analysis.one_liner: Moves the consumer financial watchdog's funding from the Federal Reserve to yearly congressional appropriations.
analysis.headline: Introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, the bill sat on the Senate calendar and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2010, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) — the agency that polices banks, credit card companies, and lenders on behalf of consumers — has been funded by automatic transfers from the Federal Reserve, rather than by money Congress votes on each year [S2][S3]. This bill would end that arrangement and put the agency's budget into the annual appropriations process, where Congress decides the funding each year [S2][S3]. Supporters of the current setup argue the independent funding was designed to keep the watchdog from being squeezed by the industries it regulates; supporters of this bill argue it makes the agency accountable to Congress like other agencies. The bill had no cosponsors, and after being read twice and placed on the Senate calendar in September 2016, it never came up for debate or a vote before the 114th Congress ended [S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, debt collectors, payday lenders, and other companies the CFPB regulates would benefit if it passed, because annual congressional funding would let lawmakers shrink or starve the agency's budget, reducing its enforcement against financial firms.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the CFPB's automatic funding from Federal Reserve System transfers and replaces it with money Congress must approve each year through the regular appropriations process [S2][S3].
It authorizes appropriations "as may be necessary" only for fiscal year 2018, so funding beyond that year would require new congressional action [S3].
Under current law, the Federal Reserve transfers allow the CFPB to be funded outside the annual appropriations process, which this bill would end [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who rely on the CFPB's oversight of financial products — the agency that handles complaints, enforcement actions, and refunds from banks, card issuers, and lenders — would bear the cost if the agency's budget could be reduced each year in the appropriations process.

drawbacks.text: A fair objection: a federal agency whose funding bypasses Congress is less accountable to elected representatives, and the bill's sponsor framed the change as subjecting the Bureau to the regular appropriations process like most other agencies [S3].

The honest cost of the current independent funding structure is that Congress cannot directly control the budget of an agency with substantial regulatory power; this bill would have given Congress that control, but that same control could be used to cut the agency's funding regardless of its performance [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim — congressional accountability over a regulator's budget — is a legitimate principle. But the CFPB's independent funding was written into the 2010 law specifically so the agency could not be defunded through lobbying pressure during the annual budget fight, and the industries most affected by the change are the ones the agency polices. The bill also offered no replacement protections, authorizing money only for one fiscal year [S3]. The practical effect would have been to give opponents of the agency a yearly lever over it, at the cost of the enforcement consumers depend on.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 13, 2016, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but no senator joined as a cosponsor and it never came to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended [S4][S5].

narrative.text: Senator David Perdue introduced the bill on September 13, 2016 [S5].
It was read the first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar, then read the second time and placed on the calendar under General Orders on September 14, 2016 [S5].
No further action was taken after September 14, 2016, and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers, who kept the CFPB's independent funding structure intact, and the agency itself, which faced no change to how it is funded; the financial industry did not get the appropriations lever this bill would have created.

for.name: Sen. David Perdue
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator sponsored the bill, no one cosponsored it, and no votes were ever recorded, so there is no roll-call or sponsorship evidence of either party's position.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and other CFPB-regulated financial firms
industries.note: The bill would have moved the agency that polices these firms onto annual congressional funding, giving lawmakers a yearly lever to shrink its budget and enforcement. Their gain would come at the direct cost of consumer protections [S2][S3].
